0.title: A. Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent
0.content: PHW.A · strict (defaulted) · 6 step(s) . Captures, updates, or revokes a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry using the IHE PCF Access Consent [ITI-108] transaction (Post, Put, Delete). Trust-anchor neutral: applicable across any trust network (including the WHO GDHCN or national/regional trust anchors) with no IUA claim. This is the person-side view of DSA process P9 (individual consent linked to the agreement). It applies only to agreements whose legal basis is consent (rule 1): treatment, public-health law and research waivers do not rest on consent. Where the person has recorded nothing, the jurisdiction’s chosen PCF implicit default policy applies, opt-in (for example Policy-deny) or opt-out (for example Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal) (rule 4) (owner consent rules, 2026-10-30 19:27Z). i i i i i i

17.doc: D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P4)
17.title: D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P4)
17.content: PHW.D · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . Registers the data recipient’s server as an OAuth client of the data provider. The client is registered dynamically, by RFC 7591 or by UDAP Dynamic Client Registration as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (X.509 certificate-based, which fits a national X.509 PKI as the trust anchor), or it is entered by an administrator. It authenticates with mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or a JWT client assertion (RFC 7523; on the UDAP route, private_key_jwt with an x5c certificate chain, SSRAA §5.2), using a key published under a trust anchor the agreement accepts, and the server records which agreement versions the client may act under. Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. Source: the data sharing agreement (DSA) process analysis for litlfred/folio-assistant#2702, §2 and §4. Not run by the engine. 20.doc: D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P4)
20.title: Steps
20.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | D1. Prepare client key or certificate under an accepted trust anchorPHW.D.1 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | The recipient uses a key pair or X.509 certificate already published under a trust anchor the agreement accepts (DSA P3). Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. | . | D2. Send dynamic client registration request (RFC 7591)PHW.D.2 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | Client registration request (RFC 7591 §3.1 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). For private_key_jwt, the metadata carries jwks or jwks_uri (RFC 7523 §2.2 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). For mutual TLS, it carries tls_client_auth and the certificate subject (RFC 8705 §2.1 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). RFC 7592 (registration management) is Experimental and needs owner approval before use. | . | D9. Discover UDAP server metadata (SSRAA §2)PHW.D.9 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | UDAP route. The client sends GET {baseURL}/.well-known/udap to the provider’s FHIR server, without client authentication (HL7 SSRAA 2.0.0 §2.1). The response is UDAP metadata as per UDAP Server Metadata STU1 §1, with the elements of SSRAA §2.2 (for example udap_versions_supported, registration_endpoint, token_endpoint, udap_certifications_required) and the signed_metadata JWT of SSRAA §2.3, which the client validates against its trust community. A 404 Not Found means the server does not support UDAP. Where the server serves more than one trust community, SSRAA §2.4 applies. UDAP approved by the owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z. | . | D10. Send UDAP registration request with signed software statement (SSRAA §3)PHW.D.10 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | UDAP route. The client POSTs software_statement, optional certifications, and udap = 1 to the registration_endpoint (HL7 SSRAA 2.0.0 §3.2.3; UDAP Dynamic Client Registration STU1 §2). The software statement is a JWT signed with the private key of the client’s X.509 certificate, which is carried in the x5c header (SSRAA §3.1, §7.1.3). Its claims are those of SSRAA §3.1: iss and sub (the client URI, which SHALL match a uniformResourceIdentifier Subject Alternative Name in the certificate), aud, exp (at most 5 minutes after iat), iat, jti, client_name, contacts, grant_types (client_credentials for a server client), token_endpoint_auth_method = private_key_jwt, and scope. Certifications and endorsements are optional unless the server lists them in udap_certifications_required (SSRAA §3.3; UDAP Certifications and Endorsements for Client Applications STU1). A later request with the same iss from the same trust community modifies the registration, and an empty grant_types cancels it (SSRAA §3.4). | . | D3. Enter client by hand, scopes from the signed agreement textPHW.D.3 | Data Provider Administrator (person) | — | Document-only route (and always allowed): the administrator registers the client_id, the mTLS certificate or JWKS, and scopes that match what the agreement allows. The change record cites the agreement’s fixed-version URL and its SHA-256. | . | D4. Validate client key or certificate against the accepted trust anchorPHW.D.4 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | — | The authorization server checks that the client’s key or certificate chains to, or is listed by, a trust anchor the agreement accepts: a DID document (did:web), an RFC 5280 certification path (§6 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)), or a local list. On the UDAP route it validates the registration request as per UDAP Dynamic Client Registration STU1 §4, as HL7 SSRAA 2.0.0 §3.2.3 requires: the software statement’s JWT payload and signature, the x5c certificate chain to an anchor of the trust community (for example a national X.509 PKI), and the requested registration parameters. | . | D5. Return trust list or certificate statusPHW.D.5 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another accepted anchor) | — | The trust anchor serves its signed trust list or certificate revocation list. GDHCN: did:web:tng-cdn.who.int:v2:trustlist with a JsonWebSignature2020 proof. X.509: CRL (RFC 5280 §5 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). | . | D7. Issue client_id (RFC 7591)PHW.D.7 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | — | Client information response with the client_id (RFC 7591 §3.2.1 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)), or the administrator hands it over. On the UDAP route the response is 201 Created as per UDAP Dynamic Client Registration STU1 §5.1, or an error as per §5.2 (HL7 SSRAA 2.0.0 §3.2.3); a modification returns the same client_id, usually with 200 OK (SSRAA §3.4). | . | D8. Read authorization server metadata (RFC 8414)PHW.D.8 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | The client reads the server’s metadata (RFC 8414 §3 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)): token endpoint, supported client authentication methods and DPoP signing algorithms. On the UDAP route the endpoints were already read from the UDAP metadata in D9, and the client authenticates at the token endpoint with a private_key_jwt Authentication Token carrying x5c and, for client_credentials, the hl7-b2b extension (SSRAA §5.2.1, §5.2.2). | .

23.title: E. Server-to-Server Access under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P5)
23.content: PHW.E · strict (defaulted) · 10 step(s) . A registered client asks the provider’s authorization server for a token. The request names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in RFC 9396 authorization_details.identifier (§2.2), and the client proves possession of its key with DPoP (RFC 9449) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705). The server decides under the agreement (process F) and issues a short-lived, key-bound token. The resource server checks the token on every call and records audit and provenance (process G). For a document-only agreement, the scopes the administrator set replace RAR details, and identifier can still carry the agreement URL for audit. Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. Source: the data sharing agreement (DSA) process analysis for litlfred/folio-assistant#2702, §2 and §4. i i i i i i i i i i

26.doc: E. Server-to-Server Access under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P5)
26.title: Steps
26.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | E1. Request token with authorization_details naming the agreement, plus DPoP proof or mTLSPHW.E.1 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | Token request with authorization_details (RFC 9396 §2). The type value is defined by the provider’s API (§2). The common fields are actions, locations, datatypes and identifier (§2.2), and identifier carries the agreement’s fixed-version URL (= the ODRL uid). That URL fixes the version, and the SHA-256 published with it (DCAT spdx:checksum) fixes the bytes. RFC 9396 has no field for the hash, and none is invented. Proof of possession: a DPoP proof JWT with jti, htm, htu and iat (RFC 9449 §4.2), or mutual TLS (RFC 8705 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). Across domains, the client first exchanges its home-domain token (RFC 8693 §2.1: subject_token, actor_token, audience, resource). The grant is a W3C VC 2.0 credential issued to the recipient under the agreement. OPEN POINT: no checked standard parameter carries that credential in a server-to-server token request. Without one, the registration recorded in D6 is the grant. | . | E2. Authenticate client (private_key_jwt or mTLS) and check DPoP proofPHW.E.2 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | — | The server authenticates the client registered in process D: a JWT client assertion (RFC 7523 §2.2 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705 §2 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). It then checks the DPoP proof (RFC 9449 §4.3 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). | . | E3. Decide access under the agreement (process F)PHW.E.3 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | calls F. Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P11) | Calls process F with the verified client, the agreement URL from identifier, the grant and the requested details. | . | E4. Issue short-lived key-bound token with granted detailsPHW.E.4 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | — | Access token bound to the client’s key: cnf with jkt (RFC 9449 §6.1), or a certificate-bound token (RFC 8705 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). The token response carries the granted authorization_details (RFC 9396 §7). The server may grant less than was asked (§7.1). | . | E5. Refuse token request (deny or unknown)PHW.E.5 | Provider Authorization Server (administrator + decision point) | — | OAuth error response (RFC 6749 §5.2 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). RFC 9396 defines the error invalid_authorization_details (§5 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). | . | E6. Call the API with token and DPoP proofPHW.E.6 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | Each API call carries the access token and a fresh DPoP proof that includes the token hash ath (RFC 9449 §4.2), or it runs over the same mutual TLS connection. | . | E7. Validate token, key binding and granted details on every callPHW.E.7 | Data Provider Resource Server (enforcement point) | — | The resource server validates the token locally or by introspection (RFC 7662 §2 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). Introspection returns authorization_details (RFC 9396 §9.2) and the key binding cnf (RFC 9449 §6.2). The request must lie inside the granted actions, locations and datatypes. | . | E8. Record audit and provenance (process G)PHW.E.8 | Data Provider Resource Server (enforcement point) | calls G. Audit, Provenance and Duty Checks under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P12) | Calls process G: a PROV-O record citing the agreement and the token id, plus an ATNA audit event where the server is grouped with ATNA. | . | E9. Return data or refusalPHW.E.9 | Data Provider Resource Server (enforcement point) | — | Returns the data on a valid call. Otherwise it returns an error (for example HTTP 401 or 403). | . | E10. Process responsePHW.E.10 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | — | The recipient processes the data under the agreement’s duties (process G records their fulfilment). | .

29.doc: F. Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P11)
29.title: F. Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P11)
29.content: PHW.F · strict (defaulted) · 10 step(s) . Decides one request under a data sharing agreement. It verifies the grant (a W3C VC 2.0 credential, verified by litlfred/smart-trust-tools against an accepted trust anchor) and checks the grant’s Bitstring Status List entry. It fetches the agreement by its fixed-version URL and checks its hash against the DCAT spdx:checksum. For a consent-based agreement, it also needs an active PCF Consent whose policy.uri equals the ODRL uid, following dcat:previousVersion across narrowing amendments. It then evaluates permits(), which returns permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. When several agreements or Consents apply to one request, each is evaluated alone and the results are combined by the DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (input/dmn/PHW.DT.AgreementAccess.dmn): by default ODRL 2.2 odrl:prohibit, so the request is permitted if at least one permits and none prohibits, and unknown is never permit. The policies’ own odrl:conflict, or a deployer’s replacement DMN decision with the same inputs and outputs, overrides the default (owner decision D, card Q-DRAIN-4, 2026-11-01 07:54Z and 07:55Z). The duties of every permitting agreement apply. The decision rule is the same for computable and document-only agreements; only where the rule comes from differs. Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. Source: the data sharing agreement (DSA) process analysis for litlfred/folio-assistant#2702, §2 and §4. Not run by the engine. 32.doc: F. Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P11)
32.title: Steps
32.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | F1. Collect inputs: verified requester, agreement version, grant, requestPHW.F.1 | Policy Decision Point (permits()) | — | Inputs: (1) the requester as verified in process D/E or I; (2) the agreement versions in force for this requester, each as its fixed-version URL (= ODRL uid), from the Sharer’s own configuration (process D step D6, or the lookup of process I step I4). RFC 9396 authorization_details[].identifier (§2.2) in process E, or SSRAA consent_policy in process I, MAY name one or more of them, which narrows the permissions the requester acts under but never removes another applicable agreement’s prohibition; (3) the grant, a W3C VC 2.0 credential. Its issuer is VC DM 2.0 §4.7, credentialSubject §4.8, validity §4.9 and credentialStatus §4.10. Its relatedResource (§5.3) cites the agreement URL with a digest. Where there is no credential, the registration from D6 stands in. (4) On whose behalf: the RFC 8693 act chain (§4.1). (5) The request: action, target, and purpose as HL7 PurposeOfUse. | . | F2. Verify the grant with smart-trust-tools against the accepted trust anchorPHW.F.2 | Policy Decision Point (permits()) | — | The grant’s proof is verified by litlfred/smart-trust-tools against the trust anchor(s) the agreement accepts. Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. | . | F3. Return trust list (DID document, X.509 roots or local list)PHW.F.3 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another accepted anchor) | — | The trust anchor serves the keys of the grant’s issuer. GDHCN serves them as a DID document; the alternatives are a national PKI’s X.509 roots, the issuer’s own did:web, or a local list. | . | F4. Check grant status in the Bitstring Status ListPHW.F.4 | Policy Decision Point (permits()) | — | Reads the grant’s status entry. statusPurpose revocation is final, and suspension can be lifted (W3C Bitstring Status List §2.1). A revoked or suspended grant gives deny. A status list that cannot be read gives unknown. | . | F5. Return status list credentialPHW.F.5 | Grant Issuer Status List (W3C Bitstring Status List) | — | The issuer serves the status list credential (W3C Bitstring Status List). | . | F6. Fetch the agreement at its fixed-version URL; check SHA-256 and statusPHW.F.6 | Policy Decision Point (permits()) | — | Fetches the agreement at its fixed-version URL and compares its SHA-256 with the catalogue’s spdx:checksum. A mismatch gives unknown. It also checks that the agreement is not terminated or superseded for new grants (DSA P14). | . | F7. Return DCAT distribution with spdx:checksum and statusPHW.F.7 | Agreement Publisher (DCAT catalogue) | — | The record is a DCAT 3 dcat:Distribution (§6.8), with dcat:downloadURL (§6.8.11) and spdx:checksum (§6.8.20; class Checksum §6.17). Status is DCAT 3 §6.4.30; its RDF term is believed to be adms:status (unverified). Versions are linked by previous version (§6.4.24) and versioning (§11). | . | F8. Search active Consents for this agreement [ITI-108] Access Consent: SearchPHW.F.8 | Policy Decision Point (permits()) | — | GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active (IHE PCF [ITI-108]). A Consent counts only when Consent.policy.uri (FHIR R4 Consent, as PCF profiles it) equals the agreement’s ODRL uid, or names an earlier version reached from it by dcat:previousVersion across amendments that only narrowed use (owner consent rule 2; fhir-harness#227/#228). Cached results end when a Consent in them is withdrawn (rule 4). | . | F9. Return matching Consents [ITI-108] Access ConsentPHW.F.9 | PCF Consent Registry | — | The PCF Consent Registry returns the matching Consent resources, each with Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . | F11. Receive permit, deny or unknown; hand the decision to audit (process G)PHW.F.11 | Policy Enforcement Point (authorization server, resource server or VHL Sharer) | — | The enforcement point applies the decision. The decision goes to process G with every agreement and Consent evaluated, which of them permitted (their duties apply), and the combining DMN decision used, by namespace, decision id, and its file’s fixed-version URL and SHA-256. | .

35.title: G. Audit, Provenance and Duty Checks under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P12)
35.content: PHW.G · strict (defaulted) · 4 step(s) . Records every decision under a data sharing agreement in two ways. The first is a W3C PROV-O record, citing the agreement as prov:used through its DCAT distribution and spdx:checksum (bean yy40), in a hash-chained log that is a labelled local extension. The second is an IHE ATNA audit event ([ITI-20] Record Audit Event), following the VHL profile’s ATNA grouping. Both cite the same agreement URL. The process also records duty fulfilment, compares duties with records, and supports periodic human review. IHE BALP needs owner approval. 40.doc: H. Revocation and Suspension under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P13)
40.title: H. Revocation and Suspension under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P13)
40.content: PHW.H · strict (defaulted) · 5 step(s) . Stops access under a data sharing agreement. Grant credentials are stopped by the W3C Bitstring Status List (revocation is final, suspension can be lifted). OAuth tokens and clients are stopped by revocation (RFC 7009) and by disabling the client. Keys are stopped by removing them from the trust list or by CRL. The decision is human and the mechanisms are computable, for computable and document-only agreements alike. Trust-anchor neutral: WHO GDHCN is one accepted anchor among others (a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list); UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA (Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG), is approved for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z), and OpenID Federation is out of scope. Source: the data sharing agreement (DSA) process analysis for litlfred/folio-assistant#2702, §2 and §4. i i i i i

46.doc: I. Decide a Verifiable Health Link Request under an Existing Data Sharing Agreement
46.title: I. Decide a Verifiable Health Link Request under an Existing Data Sharing Agreement
46.content: PHW.I · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . The VHL Sharer and the receiving organisation may already hold a data sharing agreement. When the receiver resolves a VHL ([ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest, then [ITI-68]), the Sharer authenticates it with the VHL option in use: HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), the Verifiable Credential Option, or OAuth with SSRAA (the HL7 profile of UDAP, approved by the owner on 2026-10-30 20:28Z). With SSRAA, the purpose of use can come from the purpose_of_use of the hl7-b2b extension in the receiver’s token request. The Sharer finds the agreement from that verified identity, decides under it with process F, and records an IHE ATNA audit event ([ITI-20]) citing the agreement’s fixed-version URL, the receiver, the purpose and the documents released. Revocation is process H. The VHL carries no agreement reference, and the person sharing binds the receiver to nothing. Without a verified identity, or without an agreement, the normal VHL rules govern. Owner rulings, 2026-10-30 20:01Z and 20:04Z (option A, identity lookup). Several agreements and Consents can be in force with one receiver at once (owner decision D, card Q-DRAIN-4, 2026-11-01 07:54Z): each is evaluated, one that does not cover the request is not applicable (not a deny), and the results are combined by the DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (input/dmn/PHW.DT.AgreementAccess.dmn). Its default is ODRL 2.2 odrl:prohibit: permit if at least one applicable policy permits and none prohibits. The policies’ own odrl:conflict, or a deployer’s replacement DMN decision with the same inputs and outputs, overrides it (owner, 07:55Z). The receiver MAY name one or more agreements to narrow what it acts under. Open point: no existing element names the identity-to-agreement mapping. Trust-anchor neutral, with no IUA claim. Not run by the engine. This diagram draws 1 element(s) the process interpreter does not implement. They are shown on the diagram and listed here, but workflow_start refuses to run this process until the interpreter supports them. | element | type | on | . | I4. Find the agreements and Consents in force; mark which apply | bpmn:BusinessRuleTask | — | . i i i i i i i i i

49.doc: I. Decide a Verifiable Health Link Request under an Existing Data Sharing Agreement
49.title: Steps
49.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | I1. Send Retrieve Manifest authenticated by the VHL option in usePHW.I.1 | VHL Receiver (receiving organisation or application) | — | The receiver authenticates [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest with one of VHL’s options. (a) HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421): ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.3 and §2:3.YY5.5.2, and the Sign Manifest Request Option (Volume 1 §1:XX.2.1). keyid identifies the receiver’s key in the trust list. (b) Verifiable Credential Option: ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.5. The receiver self-issues a W3C VC whose DataIntegrityProof is signed with its trust-network key. (c) OAuth with SSRAA Option: ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.4 and §2:3.YY5.5.3. SSRAA is the HL7 Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization IG, the FHIR profile of UDAP, approved by the owner on 2026-10-30 20:28Z. Once per receiver and Sharer pair, the receiver completes SSRAA Discovery and Dynamic Client Registration (SSRAA §2 and §3, the UDAP route of process D, steps D9 and D10). It then obtains an access token with the client_credentials grant, authenticating with a JWT client assertion (private_key_jwt) whose x5c header carries its X.509 certificate from the trust community PKI, and whose extensions carry the hl7-b2b object (SSRAA §5.2.1.1) with organization_id and purpose_of_use. It sends Retrieve Manifest with the access token as a Bearer token. The plain OAuth of process E is not a VHL option. Naming an agreement is optional (owner decision D, 2026-11-01 07:54Z): with SSRAA, the receiver MAY list the fixed-version URLs of one or more agreements in consent_policy of the hl7-b2b extension (SSRAA §5.2.1.1, an array of policy URIs). HTTP Message Signatures and the Verifiable Credential Option name none, and still work. Sections are those of the IHE/ITI.VHL source at commit 48201473, as snapshotted in litlfred/smart-trust-tools library/. | . | I2. Authenticate the receiver against the trust listPHW.I.2 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | — | The VHL Sharer authenticates the receiver as ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.7 step 2 requires. HTTP signatures: keyid, the signature base, Content-Digest, and freshness. VC: the DID URL in proof.verificationMethod, proofValue and proofPurpose. SSRAA (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.3): before issuing the token, the authorization server validates the JWT client assertion signature, checks that the x5c certificate chains to a trust anchor of the trust community, and checks jti against replay; the Sharer then validates the access token’s signature, expiration and scope. | . | I3. Return receiver key [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DIDPHW.I.3 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another anchor) | — | The Trust Anchor serves the receiver’s public key through [ITI-YY2]. With the SSRAA option, the receiver’s x5c certificate is validated against the trust community’s anchor; ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.3 also says the receiver’s public key is obtained from the trust list. A national X.509 PKI can be that anchor. | . | I5. Decide under every applicable agreement (process F)PHW.I.5 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | calls F. Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA P11) | Calls process F with the verified receiver, the URLs of every applicable agreement (and Consent), the receiver’s grant if any, and the request. Process F decides each one, then combines the results with the DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (or the deployer’s replacement): any deny gives deny, else any unknown gives unknown, else any permit gives permit, unless the policies declare another ODRL odrl:conflict strategy. The duties of every permitting agreement apply. A consent-based agreement still needs a matching active PCF Consent. VHL’s own authorisation checks (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.7 step 3) still apply: folder id, VHL signature, exp, revocation, and passcode. | . | I6. Return manifest and documents [ITI-YY5] /PHW.I.6 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | — | [ITI-YY5] 200 OK Bundle of the authorised DocumentReference entries. The document binaries are served by an MHD Document Responder ([ITI-68]; VHL Volume 1 §1:XX.3). | . | I7. Refuse with OperationOutcome [ITI-YY5] (deny or unknown)PHW.I.7 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | — | HTTP 403 with an OperationOutcome. | . | I8. Apply the normal VHL rules (no agreement applies)PHW.I.8 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | — | With no verified identity, ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.7 refuses with 401. With a verified receiver but no agreement, the request continues as in process C from step C5 (PCF consent). Auditing then follows VHL alone: ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.6 says SHOULD log, and §2:3.YY5.4.1.7 lists Audit Event - Accessed Health Data as MAY. | . | I9. Send ATNA audit event citing the agreement [ITI-20] Record Audit EventPHW.I.9 | VHL Sharer (enforcement and decision point) | — | The VHL profile requires the VHL Sharer and the VHL Receiver to be grouped with ATNA Secure Node or Secure Application for ITI-YY5. See VHL Volume 1 §1:XX.3, Table XX.3-1, and §1:XX.6.1 “ATNA - Audit Trail and Node Authentication”, which covers secure channel per [ITI-19] and audit logging. Data servers in processes E and G use the same grouping. The event goes to the Audit Record Repository (a data store) by [ITI-20] Record Audit Event (ITI TF-2: 3.20 (section from standing knowledge, unverified)). It cites the fixed-version URL of every agreement and Consent evaluated, which of them permitted, the combining decision used (PHW.DT.AgreementAccess, or the deployer’s replacement, by its DMN namespace and decision id and its file’s fixed-version URL and SHA-256), the receiver or requester, the purpose of use, the documents or data released, and the decision. With the SSRAA option, the purpose of use can be taken from purpose_of_use in the hl7-b2b extension of the receiver’s token request (SSRAA §5.2.1.1); which source the event records is an open point. IHE BALP (Basic Audit Log Patterns) AuditEvent patterns are Trial Implementation and need owner approval before this IG names them as conformance. The harness PROV-O record (G1) cites the same agreement URL, so the two logs agree. This is the same event as process G step G3. The PROV-O record of process G step G1 is written too, citing the same agreement. | . | I11. Process documents or refusal [ITI-YY5] responsePHW.I.11 | VHL Receiver (receiving organisation or application) | — | The receiver processes the documents, which it decrypts with the VHL key, or the refusal. | .

64.title: L. Record Explicit Consent
64.content: PHW.L · strict (defaulted) · 6 step(s) . The holder gives explicit consent by their own act (owner, 2026-11-07). The wallet, or a health worker acting as IHE PCF Consent Recorder, shows the trust domain’s consent text: a code in the domain’s terms-of-use ValueSet (TrustDomain.termsOfUse in the GDHCN Trust IG), at a stated code system version. When the holder agrees, the act is recorded as evidence and a PHWExplicitConsent is posted to the Consent Registry with IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent. When the holder does not agree, no explicit consent exists and the trust domain’s default policy applies (implied consent, PHWImpliedConsent). Trust-anchor neutral; no IUA claim. i i i i i i

117.title: Act on decision-support guidance
117.content: Process_ActOnDecisionSupport · advisory · 4 step(s) . The point-of-care system applies one of the DAK’s decision tables, published as a CPG-on-FHIR PlanDefinition, to one client ($apply) and shows the health worker what it proposes (a RequestGroup, or CDS Hooks cards). The health worker accepts or declines each action, one tap each, and the system makes the accepted requests active in the client’s CarePlan; a declined action is never written. Recording why is OPTIONAL and never blocks: after the review a parallel split (Gateway_Fork) sends the main path on to the care plan and, separately, to Gateway_AddReason, which reads whether the health worker tapped “add a reason” while reviewing (false unless they did, so skipping is the default) and only then reaches the rationale task. The two paths end at their own end events and are never joined, so the care plan never waits for documentation. That is the simplest correct construct the harness executes: a non-interrupting boundary event on the review says the same thing, but the harness’s interpreter does not run boundary events; an inclusive gateway would need a join the main path waits at; and a rationale task on the main path would make every run pass through it. The record, when made, is one FHIR Provenance. Skills: apply-decision-support, review-decision-support-guidance, record-decision-rationale, activate-accepted-guidance (package authoring-who-smart-guidelines). i i i i

123.title: Agent activity log
123.content: Process_ActivityLog · advisory · 8 step(s) . What an agent writes down about its own run, and what a person can do with it afterwards: task starts and ends, messages and errors, persisted where somebody can read them. You are in this process on every task, whether or not capture is on — the first gateway is what decides, and an agent that does not check it logs into nothing. The log operator’s lane is the other half: a person discards one entry or a whole session, and the scheduled sweep does neither on its own. This is not the work plan. beans records WHAT is being worked on and survives the session; this records what happened during it. The two answer different questions and a reader reaching for one is badly served by the other. i i i i i i i i

129.title: Actor and role administration
129.content: Process_ActorRoleAdministration · strict · 6 step(s) . Changing who can do what: adding an actor, opening or closing a role to one, granting or revoking a permission — and auditing the graph afterwards, because the declaration and the graph are two things that can disagree. You are in this process when the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to is what is changing. That is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit: a role added without an audit is a lane binding that resolves today and may not tomorrow, and nothing else in the corpus would notice. Retirement, never deletion. An actor id is referenced from commits, sidecars and other declarations, so removing one makes an old record unreadable while retiring one leaves it legible and says the actor has stopped. i i i i i i

135.title: Adapting Guidelines for Country use
135.content: . The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the guidelines for country use. To implement WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in line with local policies, procedures, and digital tools. This implementation guide provides the generic content required in digital systems, independently of a specific software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article. The standards-based technical artifacts in this implementation guide are at the third layer of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides code necessary for software developers to incorporate standardised logic from WHO guidelines into digital systems, testable for conformance to standards including fidelity to recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on operational (L2) by mapping L2 content to value sets and Health Level Seven International Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. Alongside data standards from L2, this allows for semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from guidelines, which might include clinical decision support and calculations for performance indicators, which may be encoded into Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be consistently extracted to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations in this implementation guide are intended for adaptation into countries’ digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions comprising L3 machine-readable recommendations may then be testable for conformance to interoperability standards. The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems. Edit this page on GitHub .

136.title: Adjudication
136.content: Process_Adjudication · advisory · 3 step(s) . A criterion’s reviewer entries disagree and no mechanism can settle them: this is the judgement that does, and the record it must leave. You are in this process when a sidecar holds two entries for ONE criterion that do not agree — a script failing what a reviewer passed, an agent and a person reading the same block differently. That is the entry condition and it is computable, which is why the first gateway leaves rather than guessing: one reviewer and no checker is a review, one checker and no reviewer is a gate, and neither is adjudicable. Nobody enters this process by declaring that they have entered it. Three things the diagram holds that prose kept losing. The adjudicator is DISPATCHED rather than briefed — given the findings and the checker’s output and, deliberately, never the artefact, because an adjudicator shown the artefact can talk itself into any reading of the finding and that failure raises no error. The adjudication LEADS the criterion and the checker’s entry is KEPT beneath it, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information and a sidecar showing only the winner has lost it. And the dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against by its field_hash, so it lapses when the source moves and never becomes precedent. This process ENDS at the judgement. What the answer means, and what is done about it, belongs to whoever asked — criterion-adjudication.bpmn is the QA-criterion specialisation, where the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted with its reason. Until 2026-09-23 those three lived here and every caller ran them: six diagrams called this process and only two asked a question they answer. Bean bvuk. What stays shared is what must not vary: the entry condition nobody may declare their way past, the untainted dispatch, and the restriction to a person or an agent. What a legitimate outcome IS does vary, and it now varies where it is asked. i i i

148.title: Ask the person
148.content: Process_AskThePerson · strict · 3 step(s) . The ONE way a question or decision is put to a person. Called as a subprocess from every step that asks; never run on its own. The rule it carries out is the box at the top of interaction-modality. WHY A SUBPROCESS. The rule must hold whatever the host’s question tool is called (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, a button card). One subprocess, called by every asking step, makes the association visible in the diagrams and checkable. THE ORDER IS THE RULE: the full question goes in the chat FIRST, then the card. Once answered, a card shows only the chosen option; the chat text is the only lasting record of what was asked. This holds whatever the host’s own tool guidance says. INPUT AND OUTPUT: the ask-the-person skill’s schemas, schemas/skills/ask-the-person/input.schema.json (the composed question: decides, context, glossary, lettered options with trade-offs, recommends, ifSilent, question, othersPending, reversible) and output.schema.json (asked.chat and asked.card, outcome, chosen, quote, defaultTaken). A calling step supplies the input and receives the output. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: decide. The caller owns the decision; this subprocess only gets an answer back to it, or the stated default when none comes. WHAT IS BOOTSTRAP’S AND WHAT IS OURS. The discussion itself (say what is decided and why, lay out the options with their costs, recommend one, ask ONE question, follow up narrower, apply a default only if allowed, record what is still open) is bootstrap’s Process_HumanAgentDiscussion, which cat-harness reaches through needs: ["bootstrap"], so the steps are not drawn here a second time. What this process adds is the harness’s own part: the composed question with lettered options and glossed names, the sibling hand-back, and the delivery rule that the full question goes in the chat FIRST and the card second. i i i

160.title: Close the bean
160.content: Process_BeanClose · strict · 4 step(s) . The closing half of every bean’s life: end it in a state that says why. Done work is completed and archived; unwanted work is scrapped with its reasons — never deleted — and archived; blocked work records what it waits on and goes back to todo for whoever can act. Called, never run on its own, straight before an end event of a process that called Process_BeanOpen. A bean is never deleted. A scrapped bean stops the next agent re-entering a dead end; a deleted one leaves a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. i i i i

166.title: Drain the beans
166.content: Process_BeanDrain · strict · 7 step(s) . Draining open beans with several agents at once, as part of the SDLC: build one queue grouped by owner, then take a bean, open it, work it, close it, and take the next — refilling from the deepest queue when a drainer’s list runs dry, until nothing drainable is left. You are in this process when you are asked to drain beans, when you spawn drainers, or when you pull from a shared queue next to other agents. Each bean still goes through the ordinary OPEN and CLOSE (Process_BeanOpen, Process_BeanClose); what the drain adds is the queue around them, and the rule that a bean another agent holds is skipped, not worked. The queue is advisory: it says who should take a bean, and only OPEN’s claim says who did. i i i i i i i

One agent can hold this lane and the drainer lane at once. | . | Drainer | authoring-agent | Takes beans from its own list one at a time and runs each through OPEN, the work and CLOSE before it takes the next. 172.title: Agent bean lifecycle
172.content: Process_BeanLifecycle · strict · 3 step(s) . The whole life of a work-plan item, drawn the way every bean-touching process now runs it: OPEN the bean (check before you create, find out whose it is, claim it or leave it alone), do the work keeping the body current, then CLOSE it in a state that says why (complete and archive, scrap with reasons and archive, or record the blocker and hand back). You are in this process the moment durable work is identified — which is before the first tool call, not after the work is done. The two halves are called processes, Process_BeanOpen and Process_BeanClose, so the rules live in one place: a process that works on a bean calls the first where the bean becomes its own and the second before each end it reaches from there. The one irreversible thing is refused outright. Unwanted work is SCRAPPED with its reasons, never deleted, because a scrapped bean stops the next agent re-entering a dead end while a deleted one leaves a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. i i i

184.title: Board: open and close content
184.content: Process_BoardOpenClose · advisory · 7 step(s) . What a reader does to a board and what the renderer does back: every card rests as its avatar, a window opens onto the one the reader chose, and it closes back to where it came from. You are in this process when the question is a READER’s — which card is open, what is raised, how to get back. Semantic zoom is in here too and is deliberately not the same mechanism: the threshold is resolved from the kind and applies itself by SIZE, while opening and closing are a person’s acts. The rule the diagram holds is the one about the way back: an action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. i i i i i i i

190.title: Board: place a note
190.content: Process_BoardPlaceNote · advisory · 3 step(s) . Putting a note at a spot on a board: write the note into the folio, record where it was drawn on THIS board, and sweep any position whose note has gone. You are in this process whenever a note is to appear somewhere. The first gateway exists because the note may already be there — placing is not the same as creating, and a process that conflated them would duplicate content every time somebody moved something. The rule the diagram holds is in the first activity’s own wording: the note goes into the folio WITH NO COORDINATE. A folio is complete with no board, so a coordinate on a note would make the content depend on a drawing of it. The x,y belongs to the layer, keyed to one board, and an orphaned position is swept from the LAYER rather than being allowed to keep a note alive. i i i

196.title: Board: relocate content to the trashcan
196.content: Process_BoardRelocate · strict · 5 step(s) . Moving open content to the trashcan from the board, with the reader’s confirmation in front of the move and not behind it. You are in this process when the fishbone is used on open content. The confirmation gateway has a real “nothing moved” end state, because a destructive action whose refusal is not drawn is a destructive action somebody performs by accident. The order of the two writes is the content of the diagram. The CONTENT relocates, and only then are its positions dropped and orphans swept — the folio carries what is true, the layout layer carries where it was drawn, and the arrow never runs the other way. Sweeping first would leave the board authoritative over the folio for the length of one step. i i i i i

202.title: Business Processes
202.content: . This page describes the core business processes and workflows for the Personal Health Wallet (PHW) Implementation Guide, integrating IHE IT Infrastructure Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) v1.1.0 (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/1.1.0/) and IHE IT Infrastructure Verifiable Health Links (VHL) v1.0.0-comment (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/1.0.0-comment/). A business process is a set of related activities or tasks performed together by system actors and human personas to achieve a health information exchange objective. Each workflow below is authored in BPMN 2.0 (input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn) with full BPMN Diagram Interchange (bpmndi:BPMNDiagram) layout and drawn from it to SVG (input/images/PHW.A.svg and so on) by tools/render-bpmn/render_bpmn.ts; never edit a drawing, change the BPMN. The data sharing agreement processes D to H, below, take the same form. Architectural Principles . | Trust-Anchor Neutrality: Every process models PKI key publication ([ITI-YY1]) and trust list retrieval ([ITI-YY2]) against an abstract Trust Anchor actor (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ActorDefinition/TrustAnchor). The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor implementation among others (such as national health PKI roots, regional cross-border trust networks, or bilateral federation anchors). | Explicit IHE PCF and VHL Transaction Binding: Every cross-actor task names its normative IHE transaction ([ITI-108] Access Consent, [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID, [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID, [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL, [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL, [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest). | No IHE IUA Claim: Consent management and enforcement operate over IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent and VHL [ITI-YY1]–[ITI-YY5] without claiming conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA [ITI-71]). | | Three-Valued Consent Decision and PROV-O Provenance: During VHL redemption (Process C), patient privacy consent directives retrieved via [ITI-108] are translated to W3C ODRL 2.2 policies (consentToOdrl()) and evaluated via three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown), recording a W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . | . Overview of Key Business Processes . The following table summarizes the three BPMN 2.0 consent and Verifiable Health Link business processes defined in this Implementation Guide. The data sharing agreement processes are summarized in their own section below. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Personas | Objectives | . | A | Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent | PHW.A | Holder, Consent Recorder, Consent Registry | Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry via [ITI-108] Access Consent (Post, Put, Delete). | . | B | Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link | PHW.B | Holder, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry, Trust Anchor | Register VHL Sharer signing keys with a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record active patient consent ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) stored in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. | . | C | Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement | PHW.C | Holder, VHL Receiver, Trust Anchor, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry | Present a VHL ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic trust via a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), request the manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit / deny / unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with PROV-O provenance. | . Workflows . A. Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent . | Process ID: PHW.A | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn | Objective: Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry using the IHE PCF Access Consent [ITI-108] transaction (Post, Put, Delete), trust-anchor neutral and with no IUA claim. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.A.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Select base policy & disclosure scope (PCF Basic / Intermediate Consent) | Selection of base policy (Consent.policy.uri), PCFPurposeOfUseVS purpose of use, authorized actors, validity period, and clinical data scope | . | PHW.A.2 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Construct FHIR Consent & Provenance (IHE.PCF.consentBasic / Intermediate) | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, IHE.PCF.provenance | . | PHW.A.3 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Create consent directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (POST [base]/Consent or transaction Bundle with Provenance) | . | PHW.A.4 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Update or revoke directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Put / Delete | [ITI-108] Access Consent (PUT [base]/Consent/[id] or DELETE [base]/Consent/[id]) | . | PHW.A.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Validate, version & persist Consent + Provenance [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), assigning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.A.6 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Confirm recorded Consent.id & versionId [ITI-108] Access Consent response | [ITI-108] Access Consent response (201 Created / 200 OK) | . Consent rules, from the person’s side . Process A is the person-side view of the data sharing agreement’s consent process (P9). The owner set four rules on 2026-10-30: . | Legal basis. Only an agreement whose legal basis is consent asks for consent. Treatment, public-health law and research waivers do not rest on consent. | Version pinning. The person consents to one fixed version of the agreement: Consent.policy.uri is that version’s URL. If the agreement is amended to widen use, the new version needs new consent. An amendment that narrows use does not. | Plain language. The person is shown the agreement’s plain-language summary, published and hashed with the agreement. That summary is what they consent to (task PHW.A.1). | Scale. Where the person has recorded nothing, the jurisdiction’s chosen PCF implicit default policy applies: opt-in (for example Policy-deny) or opt-out (for example Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal). Registry lookups may be cached (task PHW.C.5), but withdrawing a Consent (status becomes inactive, task PHW.A.4) ends every cached result that holds it at once. | . B. Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link . | Process ID: PHW.B | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn | Objective: Publish VHL Sharer PKI signing keys to an abstract Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record an active patient privacy consent directive ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) for storage in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others). | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.B.1 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Submit Sharer PKI signing key [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/PublishPKIMaterial) | . | PHW.B.2 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Publish key in Trust Anchor trust list [ITI-YY1] (GDHCN or other anchor) | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/CapabilityStatement/IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.B.3 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Request VHL generation [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL ($generate-vhl) | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/OperationDefinition/GenerateVHL) | . | PHW.B.4 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Query or record active Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search / Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active or POST [base]/Consent) | . | PHW.B.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent (Consent.id + versionId) [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry) | . | PHW.B.5a | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | B5a. Add the consent directives to the shared documents (process M, optional) | Optional (owner, 2026-11-07): before the VHL payload is assembled and signed, process M adds the consent directives the documents are shared under, explicit (the Consent returned at B5) or implied (the trust domain’s default policy), as consent entries listed in each document’s Advance Directives section. The copy in the document is evidence for the receiver; the Consent Registry copy is the one enforced. | . | PHW.B.6 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Assemble & sign VHL payload bound to Consent [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (IHE.VHL.VHLSharer), signing with [ITI-YY1] key material | . | PHW.B.7 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Store signed VHL in Personal Health Wallet [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL response received by VHLHolder | . C. Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement . | Process ID: PHW.C | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn | | Objective: Present a Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic signatures against a Trust Anchor’s trust list ([ITI-YY2]), request the health document manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit | deny | unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with W3C PROV-O decision provenance. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others) and makes no IUA claim. | . | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | disclosure with OperationOutcome [ITI-YY5] (deny or unknown) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (403 Forbidden OperationOutcome when decision is deny or unknown) | . | PHW.C.10 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Data Sharing Agreement Processes (Server to Server) . Processes D to H implement a data sharing agreement (DSA) between a data provider and a data recipient. Each one is a technical process from the DSA process analysis for folio-assistant#2702 (P4, P5, P11, P12 and P13). The owner chose this IG as their home on 2026-10-30 (19:59Z). They apply to every agreement, whether it is computable (a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement derived from the legal text) or document-only (a signed PDF). The only difference is where the access rule comes from: the ODRL Agreement, or a configuration an administrator sets by hand from the PDF. Two more expressions, outside the table, give evaluatedPolicies (every policy) and permittingPolicies (the applicable ones that permitted) for the duties and the audit. Why PRIORITY. The owner’s order (any deny, then any unknown, then any permit, then none applicable) is a ranking of outcomes, and PRIORITY is the DMN hit policy that returns the matching rule whose output comes first in the output’s ordered outputValues. Each rule then states one condition, and the ranking resolves overlaps; for example, a request with a deny and an unknown matches rules 1 and 3, and "deny" wins. Rules with the same output never overlap (rules 1 and 2 differ in conflictStrategy), so the result does not depend on rule order. COLLECT was not used: its aggregators (SUM, MIN, MAX, COUNT) work on numbers, so the outcomes would have to be coded as numbers that no standard defines. FIRST would also work, but it hides the ranking in the rule order. Every combination of up to three policies, with every outcome and strategy, was checked against the owner’s rule, and exactly one outcome results each time. Why only one table. Each row is decided by decide() for that policy alone (PHW.F.10, with the PCF Consent path of PHW.F.8), and applicability is a check of the ODRL target, purpose and assignee. Neither is a decision table, so there is no per-row DMN table. The DMN decision combines the rows once per request. Override 1: the policies. ODRL 2.2 lets each policy declare a conflict strategy with odrl:conflict: odrl:perm (permissions override prohibitions), odrl:prohibit (prohibitions override permissions) or odrl:invalid (the policy is void if any conflict is detected). These terms were checked against the ODRL 2.2 vocabulary and the pinned JSON-LD context (folio-assistant-core scripts/test-fixtures/dsa-contexts/odrl-2.2.context.json). When every applicable policy declares the same strategy, the table uses it. A policy that declares none counts as prohibit, the owner’s default D. If the applicable policies declare different strategies, conflictStrategy is invalid. ODRL 2.2 says a policy with several conflict values (after a merge or inheritance) is void when its rules conflict (W3C ODRL Information Model 2.2, Policy Conflict Strategy). This IG treats the applicable policies of one request as merged. The only declaration that changes an outcome is perm declared by every applicable policy. ODRL’s own default when nothing is declared is invalid, but the outcome is the same: with a conflict, invalid voids the policy and prohibit denies, and both are refused. 204.doc: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
204.title: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
204.content: Process_Cache · advisory · 9 step(s) . One optional process for every cache in the harness, used by render, CI, publish and every other consumer, whose components run in parallel where they are independent and in order where they are not. The rule every component follows is the skill cache-first-ci: a step is a pure function of its inputs; the key is DERIVED from them (cache:key, a lock digest, key.sh), never hand-listed; on a hit restore and skip, on a miss build and save; the full set still runs on main and nightly. OPTIONAL, AND SKIPPING IS ALWAYS CORRECT. Every consumer — the render pipeline, the code-quality gates, feature staging and the preview, publish, the docs-site publish, the merge train, and a committer’s local mount — may call it as a call activity, once with phase restore before its own work and once with phase save after that work came back green. A consumer that does not call it, or a run that cannot reach a store, simply builds: every component’s miss is the consumer doing its own work, so this process can cost a run time, never correctness. PARALLEL WHERE INDEPENDENT, IN ORDER WHERE NOT. The layers come first, because every other component reads mounted content. Then the prepared image and node_modules, the bun/pip downloads, the gate results and the generated sets restore side by side. Then the compiled Lean artefacts. Then the render seed (derive:publish’s writer records) and the FHIR IG ASTs side by side; the IG ASTs in their own lane, as the FHIR IG layer’s Process_IgAstCache, whose “valid for this commit?” is the component’s verify and whose AST refresh is its save. The Jekyll cache is last, because it caches the rendering of what the rest produce. ONLY WHAT THE TARGET NEEDS, ONLY WHAT IS STALE (owner, 2026-11-05: “not all rendering/CI/merge processes need all caches. be optimal in what needs caching” and “… be optimal in which caches need to be updated to perform a specific render”). A component runs only when the plan (cache:plan, the first gateway) marks it needed for this target; a component the target does not read is passed through untouched, neither restored nor refreshed. A needed component that is fresh is RESTORED, never rebuilt. A needed component that is stale, or whose staleness cannot be determined, is REFRESHED, incrementally where its node says so (the changed writers, the changed Lean modules over the restored .oleans, the IG AST delta, the moved layers), never wholesale when a delta is valid. A stale component no target here needs is left for the next target that needs it, or for main’s run. The plan and what actually happened are both reported (cached-step phase report), and the daily report flags a component restored and never read. EACH COMPONENT, BOTH PHASES. Restore: look up the derived key, verify the entry by its trust class — (a) against a reference derived from THIS tree, so a bad entry is only a miss; (a′) a bundle’s own manifest plus a source rule; (b) a committer’s verdict, honoured then re-verified off the critical path; (c) main-only entries, by exact key — and report hit, warm or miss with why. Save: only after the consumer’s work is green, only from main or into the run’s own ref scope, never from pull_request_target. Each component is a cache node in the knowledge graph (key recipe, derived inputs, producer, consumers, trust class, location, budget), and the cache viewer compares its current key with the key today’s pins imply, so staleness is computed, never claimed. i i i i i i i i i

207.doc: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
207.title: Steps
207.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Layers ref: restore / saveTask_Layers | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 1, which everything else needs. RESTORE: mount-from-lock replays the lock from refs/cat/layers/<key> (key = sha256 of the lock’s instances), verifying every layer’s tree digest, declaration and asset sha256 against the committed lock — class (a), verified against THIS tree, so a bad entry is only a miss, and a stale refs/cat/layers/main still serves every layer that did not move. SAVE: the committer (layers:publish, run by mount:remote after it changes the lock), with the re-pin train and main as fallbacks. Not wrapped in cached-step: its per-layer verify is finer than one hit. Owner role: the layers-ref session (CI speed 13). cache node: layers. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | Prepared image + node_modulesTask_Image | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 2a. RESTORE: the prepared CI image ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>-ci, keyed by .github/ci-image/key.sh (the lock, bun.lock, package.json, the recipe files, the bun version and ImageOS) — computed BEFORE anything is mounted, so it is not cache:key; cache:key --check image asserts the two agree. Each layer’s sha256 is checked as it streams and mount:lock:check re-hashes the result: class (a). SAVE: main or a dispatch only (the one job with packages: write). Owner role: the prepared-image session (CI speed 9). cache node: ci-image. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | bun / pip dependenciesTask_Deps | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 2b. RESTORE: the package managers’ download caches, keyed by the lockfile digest (bun.lock; the pip requirements file) and the tool version — never by a hand-listed version string. A restored download is re-verified by the package manager against the lockfile’s integrity hashes: class (a). SAVE: main; a PR into its own ref scope. Owner role: the integrator (CI speed 14). cache node: bun-deps, pip-deps. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | Gate results: restore / saveTask_Gates | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 2c. RESTORE: the result store (build/result-store/) and the CI cone records, by prefix — a WARM start: the cone (ci-cone.ts) then matches each stored entry exactly (fingerprint from cache:key --base, every recorded path state, every replayed git answer) and only an exact match is reported SKIPPED, never passed. A committer’s local gate record is class (b): honoured on the critical path, then re-verified off it. SAVE: main only (class c for CI’s records). Owner roles: the gate-reuse session (CI speed 8) and the committer-side session (CI speed 3). cache nodes: result-store, ci-cone, local-gate-records. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | Generated sets: QA copy, pagesTask_Sets | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 2d. RESTORE: the QA working copy and the publish-time pages, keyed by bundle-cache.sh digest (the tree and the exact tool versions). A bundle is checked against the manifest it carries AND a source rule (the source run’s head is this head, a parent, or a commit with this tree; or a main-scoped save) — class (a′), because a manifest alone proves a bundle intact, not built from these inputs. Hits across commits wait on the producers being byte-reproducible (the determinism audit). SAVE: the run that built it, recorded; main’s records are read by every branch. Owner role: the generated-sets session (CI speed 10); the preview’s copy, the preview session (CI speed 2). cache nodes: qa-working-copy, publish-pages. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | Lean .oleans: restore / saveTask_Lean | Build pipeline | compiled-artefact-cache | Component 3, after the layers (the Lean packages are mounted content). RESTORE: the compiled .oleans of each declared Lean package, keyed by the package, the toolchain AND the lake manifest (the Mathlib revision) — the manifest is part of the key, so an entry from another revision is a miss. lake build re-checks every restored module’s trace, so a stale module is rebuilt, not trusted: class (a). SAVE: main; a contributor’s warm build may be offered back (compiled-artefact-cache) and is accepted only through that same trace check. Owner role: the integrator (CI speed 14). cache node: lean-oleans. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | Render seed: writer recordsTask_RenderSeed | Build pipeline | incremental-render | Component 4a, the seed of CI’s render (owner, 2026-11-05: CI does not run render; its render is derive:publish). SAVE: main’s writer-records.yml records each publish-time writer under trace (writer-cone): its read set, the state of every path it read, and the outputs it wrote. RESTORE: a run with CAT_WRITER_SKIP=1 (a pull request, staging, the preview) skips every writer whose recorded reads all still match and puts back main’s recorded outputs; a writer whose reads moved runs. The key is the writer’s recorded read set; trust (a′): the outputs are the recording’s own, so their PROVENANCE is checked — they come only from main’s recording run, never from a run a pull request could write. Owner roles: the integrator and the preview session (CI speed 2). cache node: writer-records. It reports one line in cached-step’s format — cached-step <step>: hit\|warm\|miss (<trust>) — <why>. Key <key>. — to the job summary, which the daily hit-rate report counts. | . | FHIR IG ASTs: Process_IgAstCacheTask_IgAst | FHIR IG AST cache (the FHIR IG layer) | — | Component 4b, in its own lane: the FHIR IG layer’s IG AST cache, Process_IgAstCache (declared by that layer), integrated, not replaced. It is drawn as a task because this layer may not name a process of a layer above it; the steps are that process’s. RESTORE: read the cached AST from its branch store and judge it — that process’s “valid for this commit?” IS this component’s verify (class a: the AST is judged against this commit’s IG sources and tooling); valid → the site is built from it. 212.doc: Is CI actually working on the default branch?
212.title: Is CI actually working on the default branch?
212.content: Process_CiHealth · strict · 2 step(s) . Is CI actually working on the default branch: record each workflow’s state on one tracking issue, and fail the job only when the state could not be determined. A WORKFLOW’S OUTCOME IS INVISIBLE FROM A CHECKOUT. Bean xom7: one workflow here fired on every push to main and FAILED ALL 30 TIMES OVER TWO MONTHS with nothing in the repository saying so. This is the backstop. WEEKLY, NOT DAILY, and the cadence is an argument rather than a default: the defect is “nobody noticed for two months”, not “nobody noticed for a day”, and the session-start sweep already covers every day somebody is working. A weekly run bounds the blind spot to seven days without turning the tracking issue into a feed. Could we tell? IS NOT SIMPLY THE EXIT CODE, and that is the subtlety worth drawing. bun exits 1 on an uncaught exception as well as on a live failure, so exit 1 alone does not separate “found something red” from “crashed”. The REPORT FILE separates them: --out writes it before any exit path, so a genuine red always has one and a crash before that point does not. Exit 1 with no report is reclassified as unknown. Without that, a crash would open a tracking issue quoting a stale file. THE THIRD STATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT FAILS THE JOB. Verified 2026-09-20 by reading the if: guards: unknown runs exit 1; a finding does NOT. A repository in trouble leaves this workflow GREEN and speaks through the tracking issue, while a sweep that could not look turns the job red. That inversion is deliberate and is invisible from the run list, which is the argument for drawing it. ONE TRACKING ISSUE, EDITED IN PLACE, never a comment and never a second issue — a feed nobody reads is the failure mode a watchdog invites. On unknown the issue is left UNTOUCHED: not closed, not opened, not edited. Closing it would assert the thing the sweep just failed to establish. Ensure the tracking label exists sits AFTER Could we tell? and before the split, because both issue paths need the label — the clean path filters on it too, and on a repository where nothing has ever gone wrong it would not otherwise exist. It is skipped on unknown, where neither path runs and a label hiccup must not be what fails the job. The verdict is reported through the shared tracked-watch process (Process_TrackedWatch), with the label ci-health. Its three ends say what happened: unknown (job red, issue untouched), clean (issue closed), or found (issue opened or edited, job green). i i

217.title: Classify and code content
217.content: Process_ClassifyAndCodeContent · advisory · 5 step(s) . Classifies and codes L1 extracted statements (recommendations, implementation practices, remarks, proposed coverage exclusions) and L2 DAK slots (personas, business processes, guideline domains, conditions, interventions, medicines, GRADE ratings), following the terminology-coding methodology and the classify-and-code-content skill. The authoring agent runs terminology-lookup down the four-rung reuse-first ladder, records provenance (declared, context, inferred) and candidate status, and stages the result. A person in the l1-extraction-reviewer lane signs or rejects each exclusion proposed in exclusions.proposed.json against the printed page (sections/page-NNN.md). A person in the terminologist / ontologist lane then adjudicates the candidate codings, SKOS match precision (exactMatch vs closeMatch) and any Rung 4 local glossary candidates. i i i i i

223.title: Code change and review
223.content: Process_CodeChangeReview · strict · 12 step(s) . Getting a change to the PLATFORM from “this is needed” to merged: claim the work, branch and announce it, make the change, prove it against the platform’s own gates, and carry it through review to a merge somebody else is not left holding. You are in this process for a change to folio-assistant itself. content-change-review is the same shape for a folio’s content, and the acceptance differs: here a code reviewer judges the engineering, there a review committee judges the editorial. The loop back through “root-cause the failure” is the point of drawing this at all. Red CI is not a state you report and leave; it is a state you re-enter the process from. The same is true of a review that is not clear. i i i i i i i i i i i i

229.doc: The gates a change must pass before it can merge
229.title: The gates a change must pass before it can merge
229.content: Process_CodeQualityGates · strict · 9 step(s) . The gates a change must pass before it can merge: the jobs of the code-quality workflow, each marked hard, warn-only or not a gate, joined by one question — did every hard one pass. EVERY GATE IS INDEPENDENT, AND NOTHING IN THE YAML SAYS SO IN ONE PLACE. Bean 7yvd. The file reads as a long sequence; it is not one. NO gate declares needs: on another GATE, so they all start together and the wall-clock cost of the gates is the SLOWEST job, not the sum. The needs: in the file are on jobs that are not gates: qa-publish (arc 3fva) waits for the corpus parts of gates whatever they concluded and stores the run’s QA results on the qa-reports branch, and nothing waits for it; and every job that READS the QA working copy waits for qa-working-copy (bean jtfk), which builds it once for the run instead of once per reader. That is the single most useful thing to know before adding a gate, and it is recoverable today only by checking for needs: keys that are not there. COUNT THE # bpmn-node: DECLARATIONS rather than trusting a number here: this paragraph said SIX until 2026-09-26, by which point there were eight — typescript had been split into typescript + gates and skill-registration-chain added — and the count was wrong in the one place a reader checks the shape. THE ASYMMETRY IS THE OTHER HALF, AND IT IS THE PART THAT DOES NOT GO STALE. Exactly TWO gates report without blocking — the Rust wildcard report and the dependency advisories, both STEPS of the hygiene job since bean 7fu5 — and every other gate is HARD. (qa-publish blocks nothing either, but it is not a gate at all, so it is drawn off the join rather than counted here.) Stated that way round on purpose: the warn-only set is named and closed, so it stays true as jobs are added, whereas “four are hard” needed editing the moment a ninth gate existed. Drawing them as equal boxes would be a lie a reader would act on, so the warn-only gates are labelled as such and the gateway after the join asks specifically about the HARD ones. THE TWO WARN-ONLY GATES ARE WARN-ONLY BY DIFFERENT MECHANISMS, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT. The Rust step carries continue-on-error: true — the RUNNER discards its result. The advisories step carries no such flag: its script exits 0 in every state and keeps the three states apart in its OUTPUT instead. That is deliberate, because a warn-only step whose exit code says nothing has only its output left to distinguish found nothing from could not find out, and continue-on-error would have thrown away the one signal that still worked. continue-on-error IS NOT A DEFAULT HERE, it is a decision that has been REVERSED once already: the Python import check carried it, and the flag swallowed a failure on a missing path, so the job reported success over a check that never ran. It was removed and a new unused import now fails. The flag STILL survives on exactly one step — adding a second warn-only gate did not add a second continue-on-error, which is the history being honoured rather than an oversight. Anyone reaching for the flag should read that paragraph first. TypeScript IS ONE BOX STANDING FOR ROUGHLY THIRTY REPOSITORY GATES — workflow policy, AGENTS.md cross-references and claims, declared assets, workflow skill refs and BPMN coverage, the knowledge-graph audit, generated-docs currency, agent memory, and the ratchet that fails a check script no workflow runs. They are sequential only because one job runs them; each is independent, and bun run cat gates is the local runner derived from this job so a contributor can run the same set before pushing. Mechanical throughout. Nothing here waits on a person, which is what makes build-pipeline the right lane rather than a convenient one. i i i i i i i i i
