513.title: Glossary
513.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the instance's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. A system lane — it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, which is exactly why every decision in board-open-close.bpmn and board-relocate.bpmn sits in the reader's lane instead. It is NOT the build pipeline: it runs where the reader is, once per request, and publishes nothing.notation role/board-rendererfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Boardsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/boardsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/bootstrapfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapping Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/bootstrapping-agentfirst seen 2026-09-23status current | . | Build pipelineglossary-ledger.json | Validates, renders and publishes, and watches whether that actually worked. It carries todo-manager for the two CI-watcher dispatch points in content-change-review, which claim and note a bean and never resolve one -- claim is idempotent and note appends, both fixed programs, while deciding that a publish SUCCEEDED is the judgement this lane must not make (bean xom7: docs-site.yml failed 30 times while reporting its own exit code).notation role/build-pipelinefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Building blocksglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/building-blocksfirst seen 2026-11-05status current | . | Business analystglossary-ledger.json | Turns a stated need into a modelled requirement. A specialisation of stakeholder — accountable sign-off — but NOT judgementOnly: the exit criteria are a table it applies, and only the decision on top of them is the judgement (owner ruling, 2026-10-01). Never the tester and never the system under test. Bean 3o5b.notation role/certifierfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | CI cachesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cachefirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Clinical / scientific SMEglossary-ledger.json | Reviewer whose judgement is about the subject matter rather than the artefact. Acts by domain judgement (judgementOnly: no procedure yields the answer, which is why a person is in the lane; bean vljz).notation role/clinical-smefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Cloudflare git (Artifacts)glossary-ledger.json | A git repository hosted on Cloudflare Artifacts, not GitHub. Holds the release history: BagIt tag files, signatures, the cursor, checkpoints and run reports. A mechanical role: written to, deciding nothing.notation role/cloudflare-gitfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Cloudflare R2 and CDNglossary-ledger.json | Object storage behind the CDN. Every object is named by its SHA-256 and served with an immutable cache policy; an object already present is never written again. Also serves did.json. A mechanical role, held to the contract its skills state.notation role/cloudflare-r2-cdnfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Codeglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/codefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code listsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/code-listfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code reviewerglossary-ledger.json | Judges the knowledge graph's CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the tools graph and schema definition nodes under schemas/. Not ordinary code review: the question is whether the NODE is sound — does it declare what it is, do its references resolve, is the mechanism it advertises the one that runs — which a passing test suite does not answer. Entered by DESCENDING into Process_CodeReview.notation role/code-reviewerfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Compute authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/compute-authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Content adaptersglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/content-adaptersfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Corpusglossary-ledger.json | The versioned content store and the L1 source knowledge graph. Like the work plan, a MECHANICAL role: written to, deciding nothing, and held to the contract its skills state.notation role/corpusfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Deep researcherglossary-ledger.json | Answers a question FROM a corpus already held, and is answerable for the answer. Distinct from librarian, which decides what to capture, and from ingestion-agent, which derives structure from what was captured: both produce the corpus, and this role consumes it. Added 2026-09-23 with the doc-researcher methodology, because the accountability it names — somebody who must stand behind a synthesis and its citations — belonged to no declared role. THE LANE IT BINDS IS DRAWN IN ANOTHER INSTANCE — the Deep researcher lane of folio-assistant-core/processes/library/deep-document-research.bpmn, which names this role with <folio:role ref>. It carried a lanes[] here for about an hour on 2026-09-23 before #1168 landed and inverted the relation: a lane names its role, and a role does not list its lanes, because a general node never names its users. 758.title: Bean folio-assistant-ff09 in its processes
758.content: cat-harness-tools's work plan · beans by process · every instance . BPMN workflow instances recorded in cat-harness-tools's work plan, joined with the beans they name. Ages are measured on 2026-11-10 (UTC, the day this page was built); an instance is stalled when it is running and has not moved for more than 7 days. A finished instance is marked where it ended. Beans that no instance names are listed under "Beans in no process"; the store page has every bean. A running subprocess is followed on each instance's own page.

Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1075.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1075.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1076.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
1076.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. 1084.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1084.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1086.title: WHO guideline (L1) l1-guideline
1086.content: An L1 publication containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy, structured as the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd ed.) §12.1 "Guideline format" requires, with the SMART additions Mehl 2021 names: uniquely identified recommendations and data recommendations. Sections modelled by smart-kg L1 classes are the ones a smart-kg L1 graph of the guideline holds (bean 8pzh). semi-fixed structure · 16 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/l1-guideline.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Executive summaryexecutive-summary | required | A stand-alone summary that states the key recommendations, each with its strength and the certainty of its evidence.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — All guidelines should have an executive summary, a main body and appendices. 1214.title: Who declares each specification
1214.content: A user declares the specification it depends on; the record names no user. That is data-modelling step 8 — the dependent holds the pointer — and it is why this list cannot drift from the code: a file that stops declaring stops being listed. Four forms are read: a @conformsTo tag, a conformsTo: front-matter list, an xmlns binding, and a graph typology whose typing module declares the spec (bean u63y). Every declaration names a record on this page.

The MODEL# form is the RDF spelling of the same namespace: OMG publishes no RDF vocabulary for BPMN, so a graph that states a sequence flow’s sourceRef/targetRef or a node’s incoming/outgoing (kg-export, and bootstrap-tools’ export-graph.ts) names BPMN’s own attribute by appending # to its XML namespace — the model’s name for the relation, rather than a second one minted here (owner, 2026-09-30, bean xsqm). 1280.title: Strict, advisory — and nobody said
1280.content: Three states, not two. loadProcessModel reads an undeclared policy as strict, which is right for the engine — “a process that forgot to say is governed, not exempt” — and hides a fact a reader wants. 1288.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1288.title: WireGen: from a written intent to a reviewed, mid-fidelity wireframe
1288.content: Adopted in part, 2026-09-23, by the owner’s direction. In the owner’s words: “make methodology/utilize/integrate into existing processes. need both web and mobile layouts in usability reviews. wireframe is part of design process for adjudication”. Integrated into CRDM, 2026-10-14. crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn calls Process_WireframeDesignReview (Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built; the candidates become assets of the request’s proposal, and the requester or BA chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. See wireframe-design-review. Placed in cat-harness (owner, 2026-09-23: “put wireframe in cat-harness, not folio-assist(-core)”). The method is domain-neutral, and methodology-adoption §4 puts a domain-neutral method in the harness. It was first drafted in litlfred/ihris, and its first use was that folio’s data-model site. Issue #1023.

1289.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1289.title: What the method says (rendered faithfully)
1289.content: Section numbers below are the paper’s. | Design intent comes first, as language (§3, §5.2). A short natural-language description of what the screen is for and what it holds. | Mid-fidelity is the target (§3.1.1). The wireframe is monochrome and simplified, but it carries real content, semantic icons and interactive elements, not boxes and placeholder text. | HTML is the carrier (§3.1.2, §3.3). The screen is expressed as a UI-specific HTML-like language. Raw output is post-processed against UI guidance: icons chosen by meaning, typography, and layout guidelines (§3.3). | Evaluation is blind and comparative (§4.3). Independent raters with design background see the description and a shuffled grid of candidates, without knowing which generator produced which. They mark candidates significantly better or significantly worse. | Usefulness is asked separately (§5.2): whether a wireframe is effective for inspiration, whether it relates to the description, and whether the candidates are diverse. These are rated on a 5-point scale. | Refinement is iterative (§6). Intent, then wireframe, then a revised intent, then a revised wireframe. | .

1290.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1290.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
1290.content: |   | adopted | refused, with the reason | . | intent statement | yes: every candidate set starts from one, and it is the criterion candidates are judged against | none | . | mid-fidelity with real content | yes: real content from the folio (for iHRIS: real form classes, fields, lists) | none | . | HTML carrier + guideline post-processing | yes: wireframes are HTML, and the mechanical checks are the post-processing gate | none | . | fine-tuning an LLM on Rico / Screen2Words (§3.1, §3.2) | no | That is how the authors generate; it is not a review method. Candidates here may come from a person, an agent or any tool. The method applies to what they produce. | . | blind, shuffled comparison | yes: reviewers are not told a candidate’s author | none | . | better/worse marks and Likert ratings | the structure, not the arithmetic | methodology-adoption refuses scoring and summing. A mean of Likert ratings reads as a measurement of a judgement. Reviewers record per-criterion pass / warn / fail with a reason. | . | mobile only (the paper’s data is Android, §3.1.1) | extended: both web and mobile layouts are required in every usability review (owner, 2026-09-23) | The source’s scope is narrower than our need. We state the extension rather than claim the paper supports it. | . | the reported numbers (77.5%, the user study) | no | They describe the authors’ model and datasets. Nothing here depends on them. | .

1291.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1291.title: How it plugs into existing processes
1291.content: . | Review record: each criterion gets entries from a script (the mechanical checks), an agent and a human, in block-qa/v1 sidecars. This is folio-assistant’s existing multi-reviewer primitive. | Disagreement: when entries for one criterion disagree, the candidate set enters Process_Adjudication (sdlc/processes/adjudication.bpmn). The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and the dispensation carries its reason. | Choice between surviving candidates: a one-off choice, so it uses the decision-analysis methodology. Rejected candidates are kept with the reason they lost. | After build: the rendered result does not go through theme-ui-review.bpmn any more. Theme and UI review moved to ingestion only, by owner ruling (work item 9fdi, 2026-09-24): it runs when the graphical assets arrive, from ingest-theme.bpmn, and still requires both web and mobile layouts (#1023). A post-build visual look for a wiregen output is therefore not provided by that process — recorded so it is not assumed. | . The executable form is processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. The operating skill is wireframe-design-review. The mechanical checks are the Tool wireframe-check.

1292.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1292.title: Refusals
1292.content: . | Never review a single candidate as if it were a choice. The method is comparative; at least two candidates, or say why only one exists. | Never accept a wireframe reviewed at one viewport. A web-only or mobile-only review is incomplete, not passed. | Never show a reviewer who made a candidate. Blindness is the method’s evidence of fairness. | Never let placeholder text through. Lorem ipsum makes it a low-fidelity wireframe, and the method is about mid-fidelity. | Never average the ratings into a score. | .

1293.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1293.title: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1293.content: ← All methodologies . wiregen — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. Origin. Sidong Feng, Mingyue Yuan, Jieshan Chen, Zhenchang Xing and Chunyang Chen, “Designing with Language: Wireframing UI Design Intent with Generative Large Language Models”, arXiv:2312.07755v1 [cs.HC], 12 Dec 2023. Ingested in full at cat-harness/library/arxiv-2312.07755v1/. The source states no licence, and its licence could not be established (see check:source-licence). Ingested sources: . | library/arxiv-2312.07755v1 | . Applied by skills: . | wireframe-design-review | wireframe-viewport-check | . Node file: wiregen.md .

1294.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1294.title: ODRL 2.2: permissions as rules over a declared action graph
1294.content: Adopted 2026-09-23 (issue #1180), on the owner’s choice of permission language: “W3C ODRL 2.2 and W3C PROV-O for logging” — quoted from the docblock of schemas/content/odrl.ts. This node was written after the fact, against the held Recommendation, so the platform’s subset could be checked against the standard rather than against its own description of it.

1295.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1295.title: Its sources: what is held, what is not
1295.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | ODRL Information Model 2.2 (W3C REC, 2018) | ✅ library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | the model, its classes and every MUST quoted below | . | ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2 | ❌ not held | the Common Vocabulary actions (display, modify, …) and their includedIn; the JSON-LD context. The includedIn values in ODRL_ACTIONS are not verified against it here | . | post-REC errata | ❌ not held | none | . A caution on section references. The held sections were split by PDF page, so a section file’s body often begins with the tail of the previous section. References below use the section numbers printed in the text, not the file names.

1296.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1296.title: The load-bearing idea, in the standard’s words
1296.content: “The ODRL Information Model represents Policies that express Permissions, Prohibitions and Duties related to the usage of Asset resources. The Information Model explicitly expresses what is allowed and what is not allowed by the Policy” — §2. Its terms (§1.3): a Policy is “A group of one or more Rules”; an Action “An operation on an Asset”; a Permission “The ability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Prohibition “The inability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Duty “The obligation to exercise an agreed Action”; a Party “An entity or a collection of entities that undertake Roles in a Rule”; a Constraint “A boolean/logical expression that refines an Action and Party/Asset collection or the conditions applicable to a Rule”. Three mechanisms carry the method, and the platform uses all three: . | Actions inherit through includedIn. “a Permission or Prohibition of an encompassing Action is inherited by all Actions with an includedIn relationship”, and every action other than use and transfer “MUST have one includedIn property value” (§2.4). | Constraints conjoin. “When multiple Constraints apply to the same Rule … they are interpreted as conjunction and all MUST be satisfied” (§2.5). | Conflicts are resolved by a declared strategy: “perm: the Permissions MUST override the Prohibitions; prohibit: the Prohibitions MUST override the Permissions; invalid: the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). | . And one that makes extension legitimate: a policy may “Use an ODRL Profile that declares the supported vocabulary” (§2.1), and new actions are made by creating “an instance of an Action and define its includedIn parent Action” (§3.3).

1297.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1297.title: What this platform adopts — class by class
1297.content: | ODRL | here | where | . | Policy (Set, Offer, Agreement), uid, profile, inheritFrom, conflict | adopted; both live policies are Sets with conflict: odrl:prohibit | OdrlPolicySchema, policies/*.jsonld | . | Permission | adopted: one rule per (actor, action), migrated from the old per-actor lists | policies/folio-defaults.jsonld, policies/http-gateway.jsonld | . | Prohibition | adopted in the schema and the evaluator; no live policy states one — both files’ prohibition is [] or absent | permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts | . | Action + includedIn | adopted: the folio profile’s actions each name a broader action, ending at ODRL’s odrl:display/modify/annotate/derive/translate/execute under odrl:use | skills/permissions/permissions.json, ODRL_ACTIONS, broaderOrSelf() | . | Party — assignee, assigner | adopted as the assignee of each rule, an actor id from scenarios/actors/, plus the profile party cat-harness:anyone for an unauthenticated reader | OdrlRuleSchema, ANYONE | . | Asset — target | adopted as an optional target string | ruleApplies() | . | Constraint | adopted for three profile leftOperands — cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task, cat-harness:role — and four operators eq, neq, isAnyOf, isNoneOf, conjoined | OdrlConstraintSchema, constraintHolds() | . | Profile | profile is required; the action half of the profile is permissions.json | OdrlPolicySchema | . The evaluator is the question every caller asks — the BPMN task gate (src/workflow/authorize.ts, action perform-task), the HTTP routes (src/core/rbac.ts), and the auth_whoami tool (src/tools/auth.ts) — all through decide(), over policies loaded by src/core/access.ts.

1298.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1298.title: What it refuses or departs from, with reasons
1298.content: Each item is a place where the code differs from the held text. They are stated so nobody reads @conformsTo w3c-odrl as full conformance. | Duty, obligation, consequence, remedy — refused. No reader exists, and .strict() rejects the keys “because a rule that silently means less than it says is exactly the failure a permission file must not have” (schemas/content/odrl.ts). A Permission carrying an unfulfilled duty would be read as unconditional, which is worse than refusing it. | Refinements, AssetCollection, PartyCollection, LogicalConstraint, rightOperandReference, dataType, unit, status, implies, partOf, hasPolicy, transfer — refused, for the same reason: no reader. | target is optional; ODRL requires it. §2.6.1: “A Permission MUST have one target property value of type Asset” (Prohibition likewise, §2.6.2). Here an absent target means the instance’s whole graph. Every live rule omits it. | The default conflict strategy is prohibit; ODRL’s is invalid. §2.10: “If the conflict property is not explicitly set, the default of invalid will be used.” The code names this as “OUR rule rather than claimed as ODRL’s”; both live policies set odrl:prohibit explicitly, so the difference does not fire today. Kept by owner ruling, 2026-10-01 (work item jcet): an unstated clash denies rather than voiding the policy — a deliberate profile departure, not an oversight; odrl.test.ts pins it. | Across policies, any deny wins. decide() evaluates each policy and lets a prohibition in one beat a permission in another. ODRL’s merge rule is different — inherited conflict values are replicated and “If a Policy has multiple conflict property values … then the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). Only the child’s conflict is read by permits(). | A circular inheritFrom is tolerated, not refused. §2.9: “Inheritance MUST NOT be circular.” effectiveRules() walks with a visited set, so a cycle terminates silently instead of failing. (Cycles are deliberately allowed in the action graph — the owner’s “doensnt necc need to be rooted acyclic graph”. That sits uneasily with §2.4, which calls includedIn transitive, says “the Actions form ancestor relationships”, and requires every action to reach use or transfer; a cycle among profile actions is a departure, not a reading.) | No-match answers unknown, a third value. This node found no held text that defines the outcome when no rule matches; unknown — never permit, never deny — is the platform’s rule (Decision in schemas/content/odrl.ts), so task-authorization can report it as a finding. | Role eligibility is added on top. permits() denies a permitted request whose cat-harness:role the actor is not eligible for. That is role-model’s separation of what a lane needs from what an actor may do; it is not ODRL. | Cardinalities not enforced: an empty policy validates (§2.1: “MUST have at least one permission, prohibition, or obligation”); an Offer needs no assigner and an Agreement needs no policy-level assignee (§2.1.2, §2.1.3); and the profile IRI is never checked, although §3.2 says a processor that “does not recognise the ODRL Profile identifier(s) … MUST stop processing”. | The profile is not published as RDF. §3.3 asks that new terms “must also be defined as a skos:Concept”; permissions.json is plain JSON with id, title, description, includedIn, and the profile IRI https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/ns/folio-odrl is not shown to resolve. | .

1299.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1299.title: What ODRL is not used for here
1299.content: . | Not for source licences. ODRL’s own subject is content usage, and the natural reading would be a library entry’s licence as an ODRL Offer. That is not what happens: licence.json records a status and an SPDX id, checked by bun run cat check:source-licence (scripts/check-source-licence.ts). | Not for identity. Which login is which actor is GitHub’s answer (src/core/github-auth.ts), never a policy’s — policies/README.md. | Not for logging. That is PROV-O (schemas/content/prov.ts), chosen alongside it. | .

1300.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1300.title: Where it runs
1300.content: Schema and evaluator schemas/content/odrl.ts (tests schemas/odrl.test.ts); policies policies/ (graph typology policies, validator registered in schemas/kg/graph-typology-registry.ts); the action profile skills/permissions/permissions.json; external-schema entry external-schemas/w3c-odrl.json; the design docs/proposals/odrl-prov-actor-model.md. 1301.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1301.title: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1301.content: ← All methodologies . odrl-policies — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. What an actor may DO — may this party perform this action, here? Use it when a grant or a refusal has to be written down so a machine can evaluate it: who holds an action, scoped to a process, a task or a role, and which broader action it falls under. It answers permit, deny or nobody has said. It does NOT answer who is involved in an activity (raci), which lane an actor may act in (role-model), or how a decision is reached (kepner-tregoe, dmn). It is not used here for source licences, which are recorded as SPDX ids in each library entry’s licence.json. Origin. W3C, “ODRL Information Model 2.2”, W3C Recommendation 15 February 2018, edited by Renato Iannella and Serena Villata, produced by the W3C Permissions and Obligations Expression Working Group. The held copy is the Working Group’s own staged REC snapshot (github.com/w3c/poe), not compared byte for byte with the w3.org copy and without later errata — see the entry’s licence.json. The companion “ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2”, which the model defers to for normative serialisation and the Common Vocabulary, is NOT held. Ingested sources: . | library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | . Node file: odrl-policies.md .

1302.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1302.title: RACI — involvement, in four kinds
1302.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-09-22 (work item 2xfl): RACI is a methodology, not a house practice, so it has a node here. Until that ruling it existed only as a skill, and the methodology graph reported five nodes where a reader might reasonably expect it to report this one too.

1303.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1303.title: ⚠ The cited source backs ONE sentence of this node, and nothing else
1303.content: evidence points at Dusengumuremyi (2026), ingested 2026-09-23. It earns its place only as a secondary rendering of the four roles — its §2.1, verbatim from sections/page-002.md: . a classic project management instrument delineating four roles: Responsible (doer), Accountable (owner), Consulted (input provider), and Informed (notified). Everything else in that paper is rejected, and the rejection is load-bearing rather than fastidious. Its own Data Availability statement reads “No new datasets were generated or analyzed during this study” while its abstract claims 1,247 decision events and its §4.1 reports t(1245)=47.3, p<.001; its abstract’s headline 92.4 % detection rate appears nowhere in its findings, which say 78.4 %; and its running head claims Journal of International Business Studies “Vol. 1, 2026” while its own reference list cites that journal at vol. 53 in 2022. Work item thb1 holds the full assessment with every item checkable against the ingested pages. So: cite this source for the four letters. Never cite it for a claim about what RACI achieves. No efficacy, latency, error-rate or risk-detection statement anywhere in this repository may rest on it. That split is why evidence here is not the same kind of backing swot has. swot rests on two sources that survive reading whole; this rests on one paragraph of one paper that does not. check:methodology-evidence counts nodes with a resolvable source and will now count this one — the axis measures whether a citation resolves, not whether a reader would accept it, and conflating those is what this box exists to prevent.

1304.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1304.title: The four letters
1304.content: | letter | means | direction | . | Responsible | does the work | may be several | . | Accountable | carries the decision; answers for the outcome | exactly one | . | Consulted | asked for input before | two-way | . | Informed | told after | one-way | . The axis that makes it a method rather than a list is time and direction: C happens before and is a conversation; I happens after and is a broadcast. Collapsing them turns consultation into notification, which is the failure the letters exist to keep apart.

1305.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1305.title: Exactly one Accountable
1305.content: The method’s central constraint, and the one most often broken in practice. A chart with two A’s does not record a shared decision — it records that nobody established who answers for the outcome, and it reads as complete while doing so. Zero is also a breach, once a row claims anything at all. A half-filled row is worse than an empty one for the same reason: the chart looks answered. A row where the same party is both Accountable and Consulted is not a row with two facts in it. Asking yourself is not consultation, and that pairing is how consulted becomes a formality while the chart still reads complete.

1306.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1306.title: What RACI is not
1306.content: . | Not a decision method. A is who answers for a decision, not how it is reached. Reaching it is kepner-tregoe or dmn; recording it is madr. | Not an approval gate. Answering for an outcome and signing off on one are different acts, and a method that conflated them would let a chart stand in for a gate. | Not a permission model. What a party may do in general is a different question from who is involved in this activity, and the two cross-cut. | Not a party registry. RACI names roles in rows; it does not establish who exists. Something else has to say that first. | .

1307.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1307.title: The primary is still not held
1307.content: A secondary rendering is cited above; the primary is not, and the gap has narrowed rather than closed. literature-search’s outcome 3, recorded so the next agent does not repeat the search: nothing was found because nothing could be fetched. Measured 2026-09-22 — doi.org, pmi.org and every open-access aggregator fail through this container’s proxy; only raw.githubusercontent.com answers. Candidates worth fetching, unverified and listed as leads rather than as provenance: . | candidate | why it is a candidate | access | . | PMI, PMBOK Guide — the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) | the most commonly cited formal treatment | not open access | . | The Linear Responsibility Chart literature (Cleland & King and successors) | commonly named as the earlier form RACI descends from | books, not open access | . RACI and kepner-tregoe were in the same bucket, and RACI has left it. For both, the commonly cited sources are books and paid standards, so no open-access primary exists to fetch, and closing the gap needed either a copy or a decision to render from an open secondary — the route swot took. The owner made that decision for RACI on 2026-09-23. kepner-tregoe is still in the bucket, and the same two exits are still open to it.

1308.title: How this platform applies it

1310.title: SDLC Agentic Landscape — Mapping LLM Multi-Agent Systems to the Software Lifecycle
1310.content: Adopted from arXiv:2404.04834v4 (He, Treude, and Lo, 2025). The comprehensive survey maps the state of LLM-based multi-agent (LMA) systems across every phase of the software development lifecycle (SDLC), contrasting team architectures, collaboration topologies, and benchmark results. This node establishes the systematic cross-cutting comparison between the survey’s SDLC taxonomy and the 69 executable BPMN/DMN processes in this platform.

1314.doc: SDLC agentic landscape — mapping LLM multi-agent systems to the software development lifecycle
1314.title: 4. Key Takeaways for Agentic Platform Design
1314.content: . | Process Rigor Trumps Unconstrained Multi-Agent Chat: As He et al. demonstrate in their Tetris case study, unconstrained agent conversation (e.g. ChatDev) fails repeatedly (9 out of 10 attempts failed, with the final attempt still missing core line-clearing logic) when tasks require deep stateful logic. Folio-assistant’s deterministic process boundaries, DMN rules, and compiler shims prevent these catastrophic failures. | Hybrid Deterministic/LLM Architecture is Essential: Pure generative coding degrades with complexity. Inverting the model’s responsibility from generating whole output to generating validated rules (methodologies/hybrid-llm-deterministic.md) matches the survey’s research agenda for Phase 1 (specialized agent capability enhancement). | Multi-Agent Coordination Requires Serialized Governance: Uncoordinated agent swarms produce merge chaos and duplicated work. Folio-assistant’s work item claims and merge steward fulfill the survey’s Phase 2 vision for optimizing agent synergy and leveraging industry software engineering principles. | .

1316.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1316.title: SWOT — the two axes, and what the method refuses to do
1316.content: Adopted 2026-09-22 from two ingested sources. Unlike the other methodologies here, SWOT has no standards body and no canonical text, so “adopted whole” has to mean something narrower: this file renders secondary sources faithfully, and says so everywhere it matters. Where this text and a source differ, the source is right and this file is wrong. | source | what it carries | ingested | . | Gürel & Tat (2017), theoretical review, 13pp | the history, the variants, the criticism, a worked example | library/gurel-tat-2017-swot-analysis | . | Sammut-Bonnici & Galea (2015), Wiley Encyclopedia of Management, 9pp | the conceptual framework, the resource-based internal analysis, the practical discipline | library/sammut-bonnici-galea-2015-swot-analysis | . These are the first methodology sources in this repository a reader can actually open — the other four adopted methodologies still cite origins that resolve against nothing. They agree on the method and differ in coverage, which is why both are cited rather than one chosen. Where they overlap — the two axes, the internal/external split, the attribution of the matching matrix to Weihrich, and the judgement that SWOT only starts an analysis — they say it independently, and two independent statements are worth more than either alone. Where only one covers something, this file says which.

1317.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1317.title: The method
1317.content: SWOT crosses two axes, and the whole technique is those two axes: . |   | helpful | harmful | . | internal — attributes of the organisation | Strengths | Weaknesses | . | external — attributes of the environment | Opportunities | Threats | . The internal/external split is the load-bearing one. Gürel & Tat’s definitions, verbatim in substance: . | Organizational strengths — characteristics that give advantage over others in the industry. | Organizational weaknesses — characteristics that place the organisation at a disadvantage relative to others. | Environmental opportunities — external elements that give benefits for the organization. | Environmental threats — external elements that could cause trouble for it. | . TOWS is the step that makes it produce something . Weihrich (1982) argued the only logical starting point is opportunities and threats, because they are outside the organisation and largely beyond its control, and must be managed using its strengths and weaknesses. The matching matrix that follows is where the four lists become strategy: . |   | strengths | weaknesses | . | opportunities | SO — achieve opportunities that greatly match the strengths | WO — overcome weaknesses to attain opportunities | . | threats | ST — use strengths to reduce vulnerability to threats | WT — prevent weaknesses, to avoid becoming more susceptible to threats | . Both sources attribute this matrix to Weihrich, independently. Gürel & Tat report his 1982 argument for renaming SWOT to TOWS; Sammut-Bonnici & Galea call the matrix “Weihrich’s TOWS Matrix” and describe it as “an adaptation of the SWOT Analysis” identifying tactical strategies. Two secondary sources agreeing on an attribution is not proof, but it is the strongest thing available here, and it is a different epistemic position from the origin question below, where one source explicitly reports the attribution as unsupported. TOWS is one node with SWOT here, not a second methodology. Both sources present it as SWOT reordered plus the matching step — a development of the technique, alongside Dealtry’s Dynamic SWOT and Wheelen & Hunger’s SFAS/EFAS/IFAS tables — not as an independent method with its own origin. Splitting them would mint a methodology that cites nobody for the half that does the work. If the owner reads TOWS as separable, this is the seam to cut on.

1318.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1318.title: Where the method came from, and why that is not a settled question
1318.content: Faithfulness matters more here than anywhere else in this file, because the usual story is repeated everywhere and the source declines to endorse it. Gürel & Tat report that the origin of SWOT is uncertain. Albert S. Humphrey (2005) described a research project at Stanford Research Institute running 1960–1970, with a team including Marion Dosher, Otis Benepe and Birger Lie. The paper then states plainly that literature review shows there are no academic references supporting Humphrey’s claim, and that the emergence of SWOT is usually associated instead with Philip Selznick and with the Harvard Business School business-policy group of the 1960s. The second source does not settle it either, and its silence is the point. Sammut-Bonnici & Galea (2015) is a reference chapter in an encyclopedia of management — exactly the kind of text that would state an origin if one were settled — and it gives none. It opens on the conceptual framework and never says where SWOT came from. So the second source neither corroborates nor contradicts Humphrey: it declines to enter the question. That is worth recording rather than reading as agreement. An unbacked attribution and an attribution nobody chose to make are different states, and collapsing them would turn one source’s explicit “no academic references support this” into a consensus that does not exist. So: this file does not assert who invented SWOT. An adopted methodology that launders a contested attribution into a flat statement of fact is exactly the failure an evidence base exists to prevent — and it would be this repository’s “a count in prose is a claim rather than evidence” rule, applied to a citation.

1319.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1319.title: What only the encyclopedia chapter carries
1319.content: Four things Sammut-Bonnici & Galea supply that the review does not, each of which changes how a scan should be run rather than what SWOT is. The internal axis rests on the resource-based view. Resources (tangible and intangible inputs) combine into capabilities (the capacity to use them efficiently), which create core competences, which create competitive advantage. So a strength is not “something we are good at” — it is a link in that chain, and a scan that lists attributes without it produces a list nobody can act on. A factor can be a basic requirement rather than a strength, and this is the most practically useful thing either source says. Their example: high standards of cleanliness and hygiene are intrinsically good, but in a back-office operation they contribute nothing to competitive advantage, while in catering, pharmaceutical manufacture or hospitals they are compulsory — and being compulsory makes them a requirement, not a strength. The test they give is comparison against competitors: an attribute is a strength only relative to what others have. Cognitive inertia is a named failure mode of the external axis. Strategists read their environment through cognitive maps built from personal experience, and individual and collective maps within an industry “can be indifferent to significant economic indicators and market signals during a time when an industry is changing rapidly”. Unless refreshed by regular review of incoming information, it “can lead to the decline of an organization”. The review paper names bias in the internal listing; this names the mechanism on the external side, which is the half nobody thinks to distrust. Resource similarity and coopetition. Where competitors hold near-identical resources — the same suppliers, the same technology providers, managerial skill from a common pool — they tend to similar strategies and toward coopetition, collaborative competition that grows the industry rather than market share. Their worked case is mobile network operators. It matters to a scan because a “strength” shared by the whole industry is not a strength at all, which is the same test as the hygiene example arriving from the other direction. And it states the refusal in its own words. SWOT “is good at drawing a picture of the current internal and external state of affairs, but it does not necessarily provide a guide to the strategic action” — it is “a descriptive tool”, “not a prescriptive tool that determines the nature of strategic planning”. Two independent sources reaching that conclusion is the reason the refusal below is stated as firmly as it is.

1320.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1320.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
1320.content: methodology-adoption requires both halves, with reasons. Both are below. Adopted . | The two axes and the four quadrants, as the structure of a situation scan. | The internal and external checklists as prompts for what to look at — the source gives them by business function (marketing, R&D, management information systems, management team, operations, finance, human resources) and by category of external change (societal, governmental, economic, competitive, supplier, market). | The TOWS matching step, because a SWOT that stops at four lists produces nothing actionable, which is the source’s own central criticism of it. | Its applicability at any level — the source explicitly covers individual, organizational, national and international levels, and non-profit, educational and governmental use. | . Refused, and why . SWOT must never be used here to decide anything. This is the refusal that matters, and it comes straight from the source’s conclusion: SWOT gives managers “the raw material needed to perform more in-depth strategic analysis”, but “cannot show them how to achieve a competitive advantage”, and must not become “an end in itself, temporarily raising awareness about important issues but failing to lead to the kind of action steps necessary”. Gürel & Tat’s stated limitations, each of which is a reason this platform keeps deciding elsewhere: . | Listing is prone to bias. Writing strengths on paper “is very different from testing the organization and experiencing the strengths at work”, and the content “may be unreliable, all bound up with aspirations, biases, and hope of the individuals involved”. | It cannot prioritise. Many factors can be identified, but “quantity does not mean quality”: SWOT provides no way to rank the factors it lists. That is precisely the gap kepner-tregoe fills with MUSTs and WANTs, and a table fills with dmn. | Categorisation is genuinely ambiguous. “The same factor can be fitted in two categories. A factor can be a strength and a weakness at the same time.” Strengths not maintained become weaknesses; opportunities not taken, but taken by competitors, become threats. | It is a one-shot view of a moving target — “primarily a static assessment … like studying a single frame of a picture”, developed when “environmental conditions were still”. | Strengths may not lead to an advantage, however unique or impressive. | It is rarely deployed below the organisation level, so one scan can drive wrong strategies across units for which its factors do not hold equally. | Hill and Westbrook (1997) go further and hold that the technique “expired long ago”. The source reports this rather than endorsing it, and so does this file. | . Not adopted: the quantitative extensions. The source lists a long series of attempts to give SWOT a numeric backbone — AHP, ANP, their fuzzy variants, SMART, SMAA-O, MADM, TRIZ, evidential reasoning, contrast mining, and others. None is adopted here. Each is a separate methodology with its own literature, and pulling one in to patch SWOT’s ranking problem would be the composite this repository’s methodology-adoption forbids: “this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter” is a house method that cites nobody. When ranking is needed, use a methodology adopted for ranking.

1321.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1321.title: Where the rendering stops
1321.content: . | Two secondary sources, no primary texts. Humphrey (2005), Weihrich (1982), Dealtry (1992), Wheelen & Hunger (1998), Hill & Westbrook (1997), Mintzberg (1990), Dess et al. (1997), Sirmon et al. (2010), Ip & Koo (2004) and the rest are read through one of the two. None of their own papers is in any library here, so every attribution above is second-hand and is marked as such. Where the two sources say the same thing, this file says they agree; it does not promote agreement between two secondaries into a primary finding. | The worked examples are not rendered. Gürel & Tat work a full SWOT for an international sportswear brand; Sammut-Bonnici & Galea work a coopetition case for mobile network operators. Both are in the ingested pages; neither is repeated here, because a worked example of somebody else’s commercial analysis is not guidance. | The encyclopedia chapter’s own figures are NOT in its image set. Its templates and its Figure 5 TOWS matrix are drawn as vector content, so pdf-images placed only four raster images and all four are ResearchGate cover-page furniture — two project icons, an author thumbnail, a placeholder avatar. Recorded because an image set of four decorative items could otherwise read as “this chapter has no figures”, which is false. The figures are in the page text. | No step-by-step procedure is invented. Neither source gives one: the first is a theoretical review, the second a reference chapter offering “a toolkit of templates” rather than an ordered method. The executable process beside this file (processes/process/swot-analysis.bpmn) draws only the sequence the sources themselves state — scan external, scan internal, pool, cross, hand off — and adds no step neither source supports. | .

1322.doc: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1322.title: SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors
1322.content: ← All methodologies . swot — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. Situation analysis, before a decision — never instead of one. Use it to assemble what is true about a subject’s internal attributes and its external environment, when the point is to see the field whole rather than to choose between candidate options. Not for choosing: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence behind a health recommendation is grade, and the record of whatever is decided is madr. SWOT produces the INPUT to those; it is not a substitute for any of them. Origin. Rendered from two ingested sources. Gürel, E. & Tat, M. (2017), “SWOT Analysis: A Theoretical Review”, The Journal of International Social Research 10(51), pp. 994–1006, doi:10.17719/jisr.2017.1832 — a theoretical review, carrying the history, the variants and the criticism. And Sammut-Bonnici, T. & Galea, D. (2015), “SWOT Analysis”, Wiley Encyclopedia of Management vol. 12 (Strategic Management), doi:10.1002/9781118785317.weom120103 — a reference chapter, carrying the conceptual framework and the practical discipline. The METHOD’s own origin is contested and neither source settles it — see §”Where the method came from, and why that is not a settled question”.
